angle: Pick: Spec 3 (minimal) as the base, with the strongest parts of Spec 1 and a few from Spec 2 grafted on. Scores, 1–10 each, in the order first screen · plain language · scannability · honesty · implementation effort (10 = easiest in the ~350-line generator): Spec 1 answer-first 9 · 9 · 7 · 8 · 3 = 36. Spec 2 experiment log 8 · 7 · 7 · 7 · 5 = 34. Spec 3 minimal 8 · 7 · 9 · 8 · 7 = 39. Spec 1 answers best in words, but its six text tiles push the 12-hour list off the first screen, and its build is the heaviest (4 tabs, an archive tab, overlap checks at two sizes). Spec 2's single log is the right model, but its filter chips, seven arrow verdicts and pip string all need decoding, and its headline says production passes. Spec 3 has the fewest blocks and the cheapest build, and it is the only spec that refuses to print 'production 15/15' without a per-minute score. It still has three faults, fixed here: it draws production's engine-counter bracket on the replay axis, mixing two bases; it badges a failing run 'best so far'; and it misdates two superseded readings. Final shape: three tabs. The first screen of Overview at 1440×900 shows three answer cells beside the pass-minutes chart, with the 12-hour test list directly below. Next, Why and How-to-read follow. Results holds the evidence by load, the earlier tests, the simulation, the queue and the run log. One dated `log` list drives the cells, the chart, every table and the STANDINGS.md headline. From Spec 1: question-shaped cells, including 'What is holding us back?'; the plain-name map; 15-cell minute strips; the why-we-miss matrix; Results grouped by load under production header rows; the setup table's 'how much it matters' column; correctly dated superseded readings; build checks; the 24 h layout notice; the stale-GPU state; and chart colours checked with the validator. From Spec 2: the '✕ Not yet' lead; 'Closest' as a tag separate from the verdict; test-version divider rows; and the 'no new result for N h' flag. Checking the data turned up four problems that none of the specs handled. (a) Production has never been scored minute by minute. replay_v2.py scores only our side and no PROGRESS.md row scores production, so nothing may print or plot 'production 15/15' until it is scored. Production's own 0.05% 5xx could fail a minute under the ≤ 0.1% rule. (b) PROGRESS.md 05:55 says the median first token was ≤ 1 s in 7 minutes, which means 8 minutes failed that rule, but sla_breakdown.py says 7. Per-rule counts must therefore come from one per-minute record. (c) The Oct 1 00:48 numerics run has no PROGRESS.md row. (d) 1.67 M is a planned estimate, not a measured load. Examples assume a render at Oct 1 09:05 PDT, using progress_data.json (saved 08:49) plus PROGRESS.md rows 08:50 and 09:00.

sections.content: H1 unchanged: 'MiniMax-M3.1 on one 8×B300 node: progress toward 7 M TPM per GPU'. Under it is one generated muted line (0.9rem, wraps on phone): 'Updated Oct 1 09:05 PDT · newest result 08:50 (smaller prompt chunks: 1/15, rejected) · all times PDT · How to read this page'. Beside it is a one-line GPU state that links to #recent, in exactly one of five forms. '● Running: adopted settings at ≈1.67 M since hh:mm · result ≈ hh:mm' has an ink outline. 'Between runs since hh:mm · next: <plain name>' has a gray outline. '✕ Idle since hh:mm' has a red fill and backs the keep-GPUs-busy rule. 'Stale? running since hh:mm' has a red outline and shows when a run is older than 105 min, twice the ≈52 min between normal results (05:05→05:55, 07:05→07:58→08:50). Keep the existing aria-selected + #hash + localStorage('m31tab') script, run it first and wrap it in its own try/catch, so nothing else can break tab clicks again (the 'cannot click?' bug). Add four behaviours. (1) Legacy ids: #production or a stored 'production' opens setup and scrolls to #prod; #timeline or 'timeline' opens results and scrolls to #log; any unknown id opens overview. sections.title: Do we pass the SLA yet, how far are we, and what is holding us back?
sections.purpose: Answer the owner's recurring questions in plain words and the largest type on the page. Each answer carries a date and a link to its evidence. These cells replace the six KPI tiles and the 'Where we are' paragraph.
sections.content: Anchor #status. It is always first and shares one row with the chart. At 980 px and wider, the three cells form a 300 px column to the left of the chart. Between 640 and 980 px they form a 3-column row above a full-width chart. At 640 px or less they stack full width, followed by the narrow chart. Each cell has four parts: the question (0.85rem muted, sentence case); the lead (1.15rem semibold with proportional figures; cell 1 is the page's only hero, at 1.6rem); a body of 18 words or fewer (0.95rem, ink); and one muted 0.85rem link. No fine print, no code names, and no ≈ or ≥ in a lead. (1) 'Do we pass the SLA at any load?' → lead '✕ Not yet' (red text) → body 'No load has held all 15 minutes. Closest: 9/15 at 2.23 M (Oct 1 07:05).' → link '↳ run 07:05' to #run-v3_lp_05x_v31. Once a v3.1 run reaches 15/15, the lead becomes '✓ Yes, up to X M' (ink text, green ✓, green left border) and the body becomes 'All 15 minutes on <date time>: P% of the 7.00 M goal.' (2) 'How far from production and the 7 M goal?' → lead 'Production 4.44 M' → body 'Twice our closest load (2.23 M, still failing). The 7.00 M goal is more than 3× it.' → muted line 'On the same requests · its own engine counters read 6.27–6.64 M · why two numbers ↗' linking to #prod. This cell never shows a production minute count until production is scored minute by minute; after that its lead becomes 'Production n/15 at 4.44 M'. (3) 'What is holding us back?' → lead 'Prompt-processing speed' → body 'Estimated 2–3× slower than production's. It breaks first-token time at 2.23 M and generation speed at 3.34 M.' → link 'Why ↓ · written Oct 1 08:50' to #why. The GPU state and the next runs get no cells: they appear in the header, in the top row of the 12-hour list and in #next. Fit targets: at 1440×900, the header, this row and the first rows of the 12-hour list fit within 800 px; on a 390×844 phone, all three cells fit on the first screen.

sections.title: At what load do we pass? Minutes in SLA (of 15) at each load we sent
sections.purpose: In one picture: where our pass count collapses, where production sits on the same requests, how far off 7 M is, and which point is the newest. This is the owner's 'previous chart', and it stays at the top of Overview on every refresh.
sections.content: Anchor #chart. It sits to the right of the cells (below them under 980 px), with its h2 above it. Above the plot, left-aligned, is one CSS-only checkbox (no JS), unchecked by default: 'Show the 6 runs on the older test (v3)'. One SVG function draws two variants. The wide variant uses viewBox 720×300 and shows above 640 px. The narrow variant uses viewBox 360×300 and shows at 640 px or less: x ticks every 2 M, only the PASS, closest, production and goal labels, and the newest-run callout as a text line under the plot. Axes: y is 'Minutes in SLA (of 15)', ticks 0/5/10/15, headroom to 15.6. x is 'Load we sent: M TPM per GPU (replayed production requests, not throughput served)', ticks 0–8, with muted sub-labels 'half', '¾' and 'full' under 2.23, 3.34 and 4.42. Gridlines are 1 px --grid. Text is 13 px and ticks 12 px. Marks: (1) PASS: a 2 px --pass line at y = 15 with a 12% --pass wash above it, labelled inside left in ink 'PASS = all 15 minutes'. (2) Goal: a 2 px dashed --goal line at x = 7.00, labelled in ink 'Goal 7.00 M' at its foot, never at the top, so it cannot collide with other labels. (3) Production on the same requests: once production has a per-minute score, a 10 px --prod star with a 2 px --panel ring at (4.44, n), labelled 'Production, same requests: n/15 at 4.44 M'. Until then, a --prod star on the load axis at 4.44, with a two-line ink label up and to the right, clear of the goal line: 'Production served these requests at 4.44 M' / 'minutes not scored yet'. Never draw it at y = 15 on assumption. (4) Ours on the current test (v3.1): the best run at each tested load is an ink dot (r 5.5), and those dots are joined by a 2 px ink line (2.23 → 9, 3.34 → 1). The three runs tied at 1/15 on 3.34 resolve to the adopted 05:55 run. Labels: '9/15 · closest (07:05)' and '1/15'. Every other v3.1 run is a --muted dot (r 4, 2 px --panel ring) at its true y. Dots that share a spot are offset 11 screen px sideways, oldest on the left: today 05:05 and 08:50 sit either side of 05:55 at 1/15, and 07:58 sits alone at 0/15. (5) The newest run gets a 2 px ink ring and the chart's only callout, with a leader line: 'Latest · 08:50 · smaller prompt chunks · 1/15 · rejected'. (6) A live run is marked ▼ under the x axis at its load, labelled 'running ≈1.67 M'. (7) With the checkbox on, v3 runs appear as hollow --muted circles with no line (2.23 M: 2, 7, 0, 0, 0; 4.42 M: 0). Invalid runs are not plotted. Every point is an <a href='#run-<id>'> wrapping a transparent r 12 hit circle and a <title>, e.g. 'Oct 1 07:58 · shorter draft block (4 instead of 7) · 3.34 M · 0/15 · rejected', so it can be clicked, focused and tapped. There is no legend box, because the marks are labelled directly. One muted line under the plot covers the rest: 'Every dot is one SLA measurement: minutes in SLA out of 15. Gray dots: other changes tried at that load (hover or tap). Not shown: 1 invalid run (06:25, engine out of memory) and 6 runs on the older test v3, including 0/15 at 4.42 M (Oct 1 03:20).' Caption (muted, 0.85rem): 'Each dot is one 15-minute replay of production requests recorded Sep 30 13:10–13:25 PDT (test v3.1), run on node 0008 Oct 1 05:05–08:50 PDT. Repeat runs differ by about ±1 minute.' Colours were checked with the dataviz validator against the page's panels (#FFFFFF light, #171D24 dark). In light mode, --prod #3B5BDB and --goal #D97A00 pass every check. In dark mode, --prod is #3987e5 and --goal is #d95926, because the current #7B93FF and #F2A33A fail the dark lightness band. --pass is #0ca30c (3.35:1 light, 5.06:1 dark) and is used for marks only. Context dots use --muted (5.48:1 light, 6.98:1 dark), never --pend (2.56:1 on white). No text is drawn in --goal, --prod or --pass; --goal as text is 3.12:1.

sections.title: Why do the failing minutes fail?
sections.purpose: Say in plain words which SLA rule breaks at each load and the single cause behind it, with the counts that prove it.
sections.content: Anchor #why, after #next. At most three dated sentences: 'At 2.23 M only first-token time fails: in 5 minutes one uncached prompt of 300k+ tokens needs ≥ 15 s of processing and holds up its GPU pair, and 1 minute misses the 1 s median. At 3.34 M generation drops below 60 tokens/s in 13 of 15 minutes, because prompt processing on either GPU of a pair pauses generation on both. Both trace to prompt-processing speed: ours is an estimated 2–3× slower per request than production's (kernel profile, Oct 1 05:25).' Then a small table, 'Minutes failing each rule (of 15)', with columns Run | Median first token > 1 s | Slowest 1% > 15 s | Generation < 60 tok/s | Errors > 0.1% | Minutes in SLA. Rows: '2.23 M · Oct 1 07:05 (closest)' 1 | 5 | 0 | 0 | 9/15; '3.34 M · Oct 1 05:55 (adopted settings)' 7 | 7 | 13 | 0 | 1/15; '4.42 M · Oct 1 03:20 (older test v3)' with one merged cell, 'fails all four rules; errors in 10 minutes', then 0/15. Non-zero counts are red semibold; zeros are muted. Note under the table: 'A minute can fail several rules, so a row can add up to more than its failed minutes.' A muted stamp 'Written Oct 1 08:50' adds '· N newer results since' once a newer run exists. A <details> labelled 'Full reasoning' holds the insight text of the 05:25, 07:05 and 08:50 reflections.

One known conflict must be resolved before publishing: PROGRESS.md 05:55 says the median first token was ≤ 1 s in 7 minutes, so 8 failed, while sla_breakdown.py says 7. sections.title: How do I read this page?
sections.purpose: Define the SLA, the load, the two production numbers, the goal's basis and the test versions once, in plain words, so no panel restates them differently.
sections.content: Anchor #howto, a <details> closed by default; the header link on every tab opens it. It holds eight lines, then a load table and the glossary. (1) 'TPM per GPU = tokens processed per minute (prompt including cached, plus output) ÷ 8 GPUs, the same count production's dashboard uses.' (2) The SLA sentence, worded exactly as everywhere else: 'A minute is in SLA when the median first token (TTFT p50) arrives within 1 s, the slowest 1 in 100 (TTFT p99) within 15 s, median generation speed (decode) is at least 60 tokens/s, and errors are at most 0.1%. A load passes only when all 15 measured minutes are in SLA.' (3) 'Load we sent = the TPM per GPU that the replayed production requests ask for, not what we served. It rises by adding conversations, never by speeding up time.' (4) 'Production has two numbers. 4.44 M = production on exactly the requests our full-load replay sends; compare our runs with this. 6.27–6.64 M = production's full load per GPU on its own engine counters (Sep 30 13:29–13:34). The engines count 1.1× the requests and 1.45× the prompt tokens per request that the request logs record, for reasons not yet established. The 4.20 M in older notes is the whole hub's average per GPU over the same 15 minutes.' (5) 'The 7.00 M goal is drawn on the same basis as our runs (replayed request logs): 1.58× our full-load replay.' (6) 'Test versions: v3.1 (current, first result Oct 1 05:05) = production traffic recorded Sep 30 13:10–13:25 PDT, minus the requests production itself refused (HTTP 429), with the literal-<image> bug fixed. v3 = the same traffic before those fixes. v2 = lighter Sep 28 traffic. Compare runs only within one version.' (7) 'SIM = the teammates' synthetic benchmark (StandardKernel): a cross-check, never a ranking.' (8) 'A single run varies by about ±1 minute from run to run (v2 repeat, Sep 30: 10 vs 11). All times Pacific (PDT).' The load table (test v3.1) has columns Load sent | Share of one production node's logged traffic | Production on the same requests. Rows: '≈1.67 M (planned; exact after the run) | 3/8 | not measured'; '2.23 M | half (0.5×) | 2.24 M'; '3.34 M | ¾ (0.75×) | 3.37 M'; '4.42 M (run on v3 only) | full (1.0×) | 4.44 M'; '7.00 M goal | 1.58× | —'. After the table comes a definition list in two groups (Measuring; Changes) drawn from the glossary. Wherever a table uses TTFT, p50, p99, decode or 'load sent', the term gets an <abbr title> hover with the same text.

Each entry has: id, at (ISO, PDT), kind (run | test | finding | sim | milestone | prod), test (v3.1 | v3 | v2), label, base, load, load_planned, pass, minutes, fails {p50, p99, decode, errors}, ttft [p50, p90, p99], decode, hit, errors [n, of], accept, prod {load, ttft, decode, hit, pass}, verdict, why (≤ 40 words), detail (full original text), evidence {run_id, progress, file}, superseded_by. New keys: sla; current_test; test_versions; load_levels; labels (tag → plain name); production {same_requests by test and load, engine_counters, hub_window, fleet, highest_reported, superseded[]}; setup_compare (replaces frontier_rt and prod_profile); setup_current (the adopted settings, each with adopted_at and run_id; it drives 'Adopted'); why_we_miss; layout_notice; glossary [group, term, definition]; launch_cmd.ours_now. queued gains kind, state, closed_at, outcome, plain_name, ref and needs_ok. Retired keys move to progress_data_archive.json: kpis, summary, running, metrics, tests, configs, pareto, routeb, staircase, setups, profiles, profile_rows, prod_profile, comparison, matrix, realtraffic_rank(_note), realtraffic_best, protocol_v2, chart_note, pareto_note, prod, prod_per_gpu, launch_specs[1–4] with their launch_cmd entries, and the timeline rows before Sep 29 16:15. A one-time migrate_log.py, reviewed by hand, does the move and the dating. progress_page.py targets about 420 lines after deleting about 150 lines of dead code: winning, versus_panel, comparison, matrix_panel, routeb, staircase, realtraffic_rank_panel, protocol_panel, charts, the c1/c2 JS with its embedded configs and pareto JSON, and derive_frontier. Helpers: pdt(); m2() for 2-decimal M; ttft_fmt() (2 decimals below 10 s, 1 above); half_up() for integers (76.5 → 77; Python's round() gives 76, so never use it for display); badge(); strip(). Core: status() and status_text(); node_state(); one run_table(rows, cols, group_by) shared by the 12-hour list, the v3.1/v3/v2 tables and the run log; chart(variant), called twice. Then answer_cells(), next_box(), why(), howto(), prod(), setup(), gap(), launch(), standings() and checks(). The JS is the existing tab script plus the legacy-id map, hash-to-hidden-tab and notice dismissal. CSS: tokens --prod, --goal and --pass with the validated dark values; .prodcol replaces the nth-child tint; td.k wraps at max-width 260 px; one-word .v badges that may wrap; cards at 640 px or less; the .kpi rules are deleted. update_progress.sh gains one ssh to 0008 that writes node_state.txt, and an scp of /data01/minimax31/bench/run_minutes.json. On the node, run_minutes.py (sla_breakdown.py extended) writes that file. For every replay output it gives per-minute pass/fail codes for our side and for production's own timings (prod_ttft, prod_total, prod_completion_tokens, prod_status). It checks prod_status first, because a 429 record has zero tokens. It uses replay_v2.py's own q() and SLA test, so every count matches the replay's n/15.

wording_rules: Answer first, number second: '✕ Not yet: closest 9/15 at 2.23 M', never '≈2.2 M best'. Say 'passes' only for 15/15. Never call a failing load capacity, throughput, frontier or best; say 'closest' or 'load we sent'.

Every throughput names its basis: '2.23 M sent (v3.1)', '4.44 M (production, same requests)', '6.27–6.64 M (production's engine counters, Sep 30)', 'SIM 3.34 M (simulation, no SLA)'. 'M' always means million tokens per minute per GPU. Always two decimals (2.23, never 2.2). Use '≈' only on planned or estimated values (≈1.67 M planned), never on measured ones.

Production gets a minute count only after it has been scored minute by minute with the same rule. Until then write 'met the SLA over the window'. Never write '15/15' or 'passes' for production, and never draw its star at y = 15.
Minutes: 'n/15' in tables and on the chart, 'n of 15 minutes' in sentences. Put the 15-cell strip next to n/15 wherever per-minute data exists. Minutes are numbered 0–14, as in the replay output.

Name loads by value, '3.34 M' first. Use 'half / ¾ / full load' only in group headers and sentences, and multiples (0.5×) only in the How-to-read load table. Never compare a multiple across test versions: half load is 1.36 M on v2 and 2.23 M on v3.1.

Badges are one word from a fixed list, each with an icon or shape so colour is never the only cue: ✓ Passes · Adopted (solid ink) · Baseline (ink outline) · Rejected (gray outline) · ✕ Invalid (red dashed) · Finding (dashed) · SIM (gray dashed) · ● Running · Queued · Production (blue outline) · Superseded. Tag: ◆ Closest. Action: ! Needs your OK (inverted ink). Reasons go in the row text, never in a badge. 'Adopted' means 'in the adopted settings now', so an old 'keep' that is no longer in the setup shows as Rejected with its reason.

Use plain names on Overview. Run ids, chain names, env vars and kernel or function names appear only inside <details>, as a muted 'ref'. Map: mem 0.68 → 0.76 = 'more KV-cache memory'; DSpark block 4 = 'shorter draft block (4 instead of 7)'; chunk 16384 = 'smaller prompt chunks (16k)'; fair chunk share = 'fair prompt sharing'; LPM = 'cache-first scheduling'; MAXREQ 128 = '128 requests per engine'; ROUTE_PIN_BY_INFLIGHT = 'load-aware session routing'; Dynamo KV router = 'production's router (Dynamo)'; training-off + FP8 KV = 'production-style numerics (8-bit KV cache)'; MSA = 'MiniMax's prompt-attention kernel'; OOM guard = 'out-of-memory guard'; frontier = 'adopted settings'; lever = 'change'; offered = 'sent'; knee = 'where passing collapses'; binding axis = 'the rule that fails most'; DP rank = 'GPU of a pair'.
Overview sentences say 'first token', 'generation speed' and 'prompt processing'. Tables may use TTFT p50 / TTFT p99 / decode, wrapped in <abbr> titles that carry the glossary text.

Times are Pacific: 'Oct 1 07:05', or '07:05' inside a day group. Convert UTC node logs. Never write 'today', 'now', 'this morning' or 'current' without a timestamp. Keep when traffic was recorded ('recorded Sep 30 13:10–13:25') separate from when a result landed ('run Oct 1 07:05').

State the SLA in one sentence, word for word, wherever it appears (How to read, STANDINGS.md, linked from the chart caption), with one error threshold: ≤ 0.1%, matching replay_v2.py --sla 1.0,15,60,0.001.

Each colour has one meaning. Green = passes (15/15, the PASS band, a passing minute). Red = breaks the SLA, invalid, or 'Not yet'. Gray = rejected, older or context. Blue = production. Orange = the 7 M goal. Ink = our best-per-load line and the closest run. A 9/15 is never green. Only red may colour text (6.1–6.6:1); blue, orange and green appear only as marks, borders and icons next to ink text.

Length caps: an answer-cell body is 18 words or fewer; a 12-hour row name is 8 words or fewer; a reason is 40 words or fewer and sits behind <details>; no paragraph outside <details> runs over 60 words. HTML text is never below 0.85rem; SVG labels are 13 px and ticks 12 px.

Rounding: TPM to 2 decimals. TTFT to 2 decimals below 10 s and 1 decimal from 10 s. Decode as an integer rounded half up (76.5 → 77; Python's round() gives 76, so don't use it for display). Percentages to 1 decimal.

Tag evidence. Every Overview number links to the row that produced it (#run-<id>). Every expanded row ends with 'Source: run <id> · PROGRESS.md <date time>'. Single runs carry '±1 minute run to run'. A figure that cannot be verified says 'cannot be re-checked' and why.

Derive, never type. The answer cells, chart points, counts, GPU state, next items, verdict tallies and the STANDINGS.md headline come from log, setup_current and node_state. Only why_we_miss, labels, notes and the setup table's 'how much it matters' column are written by hand. The page marks why_we_miss when a newer result exists.
Simulation numbers always carry 'SIM' and gray styling, and never appear on the answer cells or the chart.

Keep the layout stable. The Overview order and anchors (#status, #chart, #recent, #next, #why, #howto) never change between refreshes. Announce any structural change in the 24 h notice. Retired content goes to progress_data_archive.json and PROGRESS.md, with a pointer line on the page, and never silently disappears.
glossary: TPM per GPU (M): million tokens processed per minute (prompt including cached, plus output) divided by the node's 8 GPUs. Production's dashboard counts the same way.
Load we sent: the TPM per GPU that the replayed production requests ask for. It is what we offered, not what we served within the SLA.

Half / ¾ / full load: 2.23 / 3.34 / 4.42 M on test v3.1, which is 1/2, 3/4 and all of one production node's share of the logged traffic. Load is raised by adding conversations, never by speeding up time.
Minute in SLA: a minute where the median first token arrives within 1 s, the slowest 1 in 100 within 15 s, median generation speed is at least 60 tokens/s and errors are at most 0.1%.
Passes (15/15): all 15 measured minutes are in SLA. 14/15 is a fail.
Closest: the run with the most minutes in SLA on the current test (9/15 at 2.23 M, Oct 1 07:05). It is still a fail.
First token (TTFT), p50 / p99: seconds until the first output token, for the median request and for the slowest 1 in 100.
Generation speed (decode): output tokens per second for one request while it streams.
Prompt processing (prefill): reading the prompt before the first token. An uncached ('cold') prompt has to be processed in full; one of 300k tokens takes 15 s or more on our engine.
Cache hit: the share of prompt tokens already held from earlier turns of the same conversation. Production's figure for the same requests is shown in brackets.
KV-cache memory (0.68 → 0.76): the share of GPU memory kept for processed prompts. More of it means fewer conversations get evicted and processed again.
GPU pair (DP ranks): each of our 4 engines uses 2 GPUs whose attention halves step together, so a long prompt on one pauses generation on both. Production's layout avoids this.

Test v3.1 / v3 / v2: v3.1 (current) replays production traffic recorded Sep 30 13:10–13:25 PDT, minus the requests production itself refused, with the literal-<image> bug fixed. v3 is the same traffic before those fixes. v2 is lighter Sep 28 traffic. Compare runs only within one version.
Production, same requests: how production served exactly the requests we replay, according to its request logs (4.44 M at full load). It has not yet been scored minute by minute.

Production's engine counters: the token counters on production's own engines, 6.27–6.64 M per GPU on Sep 30. They count 1.45× more prompt tokens per request than the request logs; the cause is not established.
Request logs (hub logs): production's per-request logs, which our replay is built from. They show less load than the engines count.

Adopted settings (formerly 'frontier'): the setup every change is tested on top of. It is 4 engines × 2 GPUs, load-aware session routing, KV-cache memory 0.76, 32k prompt chunks, 64 requests per engine and draft block 7.
Change (formerly 'lever'): one setting or code change, tested on top of the adopted settings at one load.

Verdicts: Adopted = in the adopted settings now. Rejected = tried and dropped; the reason is in the row. Baseline = a reference run with nothing changed. Invalid = the run broke and its result does not count. Finding = an analysis, kernel test or quality test with no SLA run. SIM = a simulation.
Load-aware session routing: our gateway keeps each conversation on the same GPU pair so its cache is reused, and sends new conversations to the least-busy pair.
Production's router (Dynamo): the cache-aware router production uses. On our layout it lost cache hits (65–71% vs our 94%), so we route with our own gateway.
Draft block (DSpark): our speculative decoding. A small draft model proposes 7 tokens and the main model checks them in one step. Production uses a different draft (DFlash2) with block 4.

MiniMax's prompt-attention kernel (MSA): MiniMax's sparse-attention kernel for prompt processing. In a standalone test (Oct 1 08:02) it was 1.9–2.5× faster than ours with identical output. It does not run inside our engine yet.
Where passing collapses (formerly 'knee'): the load between a mostly passing run and a mostly failing one. On Oct 1 it lies between 2.23 M (9/15) and 3.34 M (1/15).
SIM (simulation): the teammates' StandardKernel benchmark on synthetic or recorded agent sessions. It is a cross-check and never ranks changes.
